clue.text: Nobel prizewinner whose Ashes are preserved

definitions.text: Nobel prizewinner whose Ashes are preserved

parts.words: Nobel prizewinner whose Ashes are preserved
parts.note: points to the Sardinian Nobel laureate of 1926, author of the novel Cenere, whose title means Ashes; it sounds like a cremation story

explanation.surface: A Nobel laureate's remains are kept in an urn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ashes' has a capital because it is a book title (Cenere, 1904), not a cremation; the novel is still in print, so preserved.
explanation.definitionFit: Grazia Deledda, Italian novelist, won the 1926 Nobel Prize in Literature and wrote Cenere (Ashes).

clue.text: A bird myth rewritten as boisterous song

indicators.note: words that are rewritten are set down again in a new order, so these letters get shuffled

explanation.surface: An ancient bird legend is reworked into a rowdy hymn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewritten' shuffles the nine letters of A BIRD MYTH.
explanation.definitionFit: A dithyramb was a wild choral hymn to Dionysus, hence any frenzied or boisterous poem or chant.

clue.text: King supports the French brandy provided by evolutionist

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece stands beneath the others

parts.note: la is a French word for 'the'
marc is a brandy distilled from grape pressings
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A monarch props up a French brandy supplied by a biologist.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'supports' puts K underneath LA and MARC.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed an early theory of evolution through inherited characteristics.

clue.text: Minor poet introduced by James

parts.note: a crime writer named James created a detective who also publishes verse, so a poet she brought into fiction

explanation.surface: A lesser versifier is presented by someone called James.
explanation.walkthrough: James is P. D. James, not a literary sponsor; her detective Adam Dalgliesh of Scotland Yard is a published poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Dalgliesh, P. D. James's police commander, writes poetry in the novels.

clue.text: Associated with Shaw's man

parts.note: Shaw wrote a comedy whose title pairs a soldier's weapons with the man, so the word joined to man in that title

explanation.surface: Something linked to a playwright's fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's play is Arms and the Man (1894), its title from Virgil's opening line.
explanation.definitionFit: In the title Arms and the Man, weapons are the word coupled with the man.

clue.text: English playwright associated with Horace

parts.note: Horace looks like the Latin poet, but it is the dramatist's own first name

explanation.surface: An English dramatist linked to the Roman poet of the Odes.
explanation.walkthrough: Horace Annesley Vachell (1861-1955) wrote plays and novels; 'associated' because Horace is his forename.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace Annesley Vachell was an English dramatist and novelist, author of the play Quinneys'.

clue.text: Novelist gets sort of start in VAT

indicators.note: the vat gets the jumble put into it, so it holds the other letters
a sort of start is a loose version of it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A writer receives a kind of beginning inside a tax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets' is the container signal here: the tax holds the jumbled letters made by 'sort of'. Peter Vansittart wrote historical novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Vansittart (1920-2008) was a prolific English historical novelist.

clue.text: Container for a collection of Walton's essays?

definitions.text: Container for a collection of Walton's essays?

parts.words: Container for a collection of Walton's essays?
parts.note: Izaak Walton's famous book is about angling, so his 'essays' are attempts at fishing and their haul goes in an angler's basket

explanation.surface: A box to keep a set of Walton's literary pieces in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'essays' is used in its old sense of attempts: Walton's The Compleat Angler is about fishing, and a fisher keeps the catch in a wicker basket.
explanation.definitionFit: A creel is a wicker basket in which an angler carries caught fish.

clue.text: "I've put in so many —— and puzzles that it will keep the professors busy for centuries." (Joyce)

definitions.text: "I've put in so many —— and puzzles that it will keep the professors busy for centuries." (Joyce)

parts.words: "I've put in so many —— and puzzles that it will keep the professors busy for centuries." (Joyce)
parts.note: Joyce's boast about Ulysses: the missing word pairs with puzzles as riddling things put in the book

explanation.surface: Joyce boasting that Ulysses will occupy scholars for centuries.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce said he had filled Ulysses with riddles, mysteries placed alongside puzzles for academics to work out.

clue.text: Record article describing Hogg's Miss Arabella

parts.note: a log is a written record, as of a voyage
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A written account describing a lady from a Scottish novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' is just a link. Hogg is James Hogg, author of The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Arabella Logan is a character in James Hogg's Confessions of a Justified Sinner.

clue.text: Language used in Magna Carta, militarily speaking

indicators.note: the letters are used inside the run of words Carta, militarily, spanning the comma

explanation.surface: A tongue employed in the Magna Carta, speaking in military terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used in' signals letters within CarTA MILitarily.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamil is a Dravidian tongue spoken in southern India and Sri Lanka.

clue.text: Motorway queen gets on the bypass for Scott hero

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in British road names like the M1
Anne was Queen of Great Britain 1702-14
a ring road is a bypass round a town

explanation.surface: A queen takes the motorway onto the bypass to meet a novel's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets on' joins the pieces. A RING road circles a British town, like a bypass.
explanation.definitionFit: Guy Mannering is the title character of Walter Scott's 1815 novel.

clue.text: Quickly expressed by Alonso's master

definitions.meaning: an old nautical word for briskly or promptly
in The Tempest the ship's Master, carrying King Alonso, orders the crew to work this way

explanation.definitionFit: Yarely is an archaic adverb meaning briskly; the Master in The Tempest shouts 'fall to't, yarely'.

clue.text: They were on form in Tennyson

definitions.text: They were on form in Tennyson

parts.words: They were on form in Tennyson
parts.note: a Tennyson poem orders volunteer soldiers to fall in, its title being a call to form up

explanation.surface: People who played well in a Tennyson poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on form' sounds like playing well, but Tennyson's 1859 poem is titled Riflemen Form!
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's patriotic poem Riflemen Form! called on volunteer marksmen to muster.

clue.text: Young offender of the Irish theatre

definitions.meaning: a lad sent to a British youth detention centre
Brendan Behan's memoir was adapted for the Dublin stage

explanation.definitionFit: A borstal was a British reformatory for juvenile delinquents; Brendan Behan's Borstal Boy became an Abbey Theatre play.

clue.text: Location of Hamlet's ungarter'd stocking

parts.note: Ophelia describes Hamlet with his stockings fallen down, 'down-gyved' to a joint of the leg

explanation.surface: Where the prince's loose hosiery ended up.
explanation.walkthrough: Ophelia reports Hamlet's stockings 'ungarter'd and down-gyved' to this joint (Hamlet II.i).
explanation.definitionFit: The stockings slipped down to the joint between leg and foot, as Ophelia says.

clue.text: They do their crosswords in ink, said Clement K. Shorter

definitions.text: They do their crosswords in ink, said Clement K. Shorter

parts.words: They do their crosswords in ink, said Clement K. Shorter
parts.note: the journalist Shorter's quip about solvers so confident of being right that they use a pen

explanation.surface: An editor's quip about people who fill in puzzles with a pen.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing in ink assumes no mistakes, the mark of hopeful, confident people.

clue.text: Frosty wind made moan in Christina Rossetti's

definitions.text: Frosty wind made moan in Christina Rossetti's

parts.words: Frosty wind made moan in Christina Rossetti's
parts.note: the second line of Rossetti's carol, whose title names the bleak depth of the cold season

explanation.surface: An icy wind groaned in a poem by Christina Rossetti.
explanation.walkthrough: Rossetti's carol In the Bleak Midwinter continues 'Frosty wind made moan'.
explanation.definitionFit: The carol's title season is the middle of winter, around the solstice.

clue.text: Scandalmongering lady operating on surface

parts.note: a gossip from Sheridan's comedy, whose name says she curls her lip skilfully, a look worn on the face

explanation.surface: A gossiping woman who works on appearances.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Sneerwell leads the gossips in Sheridan's The School for Scandal; a sneer is a facial look, so she operates on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Sneerwell runs the scandal-spreading circle in Sheridan's play.

clue.text: Instrument of legal cross-dressing in Venice

definitions.text: Instrument of legal cross-dressing in Venice

parts.words: Instrument of legal cross-dressing in Venice
parts.note: in The Merchant of Venice Portia disguises herself as a male lawyer under an assumed name

explanation.surface: A tool for lawful disguise in the Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Portia appears in court disguised as the young doctor of law Balthasar; 'instrument' suggests a legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: Balthasar is the false identity Portia adopts as a lawyer in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Constant critic

parts.note: reads as someone always finding fault, but Constant is a first name: an English composer who wrote music criticism

explanation.definitionFit: Constant Lambert, English composer, wrote the critical study Music Ho!

clue.text: Poet finished about noon

indicators.note: the word for finished is put about the letter, holding it

parts.note: done means finished

explanation.surface: A poet who stopped work around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts N inside DONE.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne was the leading English metaphysical poet.

clue.text: Clemency is associated with Dickens's: with Thackeray's Barnes — meanness of spirit

definitions.text: Clemency is associated with Dickens's: with Thackeray's Barnes — meanness of spirit

parts.words: Clemency is associated with Dickens's: with Thackeray's Barnes — meanness of spirit
parts.note: a surname shared by a kindly servant in Dickens's The Battle of Life, first name Clemency, and Thackeray's spiteful Barnes

explanation.surface: Mercy goes with one novelist's character, meanness with another's.
explanation.walkthrough: Clemency looks like the virtue but is a first name: Clemency Newcome in The Battle of Life; Barnes Newcome is the mean-spirited cousin in Thackeray's The Newcomes.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Clemency and Thackeray's Barnes share the same family name.

clue.text: One of Greene's stand-ups?

parts.note: Graham Greene wrote a Haiti novel whose plural title names performers who make audiences laugh

explanation.surface: One of Graham Greene's live acts.
explanation.walkthrough: Greene's novel is The Comedians (1966); a stand-up does solo comic routines.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-up is a solo comic performer.

clue.text: They are worth seeing, they say (in quotes) ()

indicators.note: they say means the word is as people pronounce it, so a word that sounds alike

parts.note: sights are places worth seeing for a tourist

explanation.surface: Places worth a visit, people report, in quotation marks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'they say' gives a word sounding like SIGHTS; the empty brackets stand for a letter count left out in print.
explanation.definitionFit: To cite is to quote a passage or author as authority.

clue.text: Stitched up by Beryl Bainbridge's protagonist?

definitions.text: Stitched up by Beryl Bainbridge's protagonist?

parts.words: Stitched up by Beryl Bainbridge's protagonist?
parts.note: Bainbridge's novel is about a seamstress, so something she would sew; stitched up sounds like framed

explanation.surface: Framed by a novel's leading character.
explanation.walkthrough: Beryl Bainbridge wrote The Dressmaker (1973); 'stitched up' usually means framed or cheated.
explanation.definitionFit: A dressmaker sews a frock, the garment made by Bainbridge's title character.

clue.text: What Mr Emerson somewhat indecorously felt Lucy Honeychurch should be?

definitions.text: What Mr Emerson somewhat indecorously felt Lucy Honeychurch should be?

parts.words: What Mr Emerson somewhat indecorously felt Lucy Honeychurch should be?
parts.note: in Forster's A Room with a View old Mr Emerson insists Lucy should have the room overlooking the Arno, so one who looks out

explanation.surface: Mr Emerson's improper idea of what Lucy ought to become.
explanation.walkthrough: In A Room with a View Mr Emerson tactlessly offers to swap rooms so Lucy can have the view; 'indecorously' hints at the breach of manners.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a room overlooking the scenery is an onlooker.

clue.text: "My virtue's still far too small, I don't — it out and about yet" (Colette)

definitions.text: "My virtue's still far too small, I don't — it out and about yet" (Colette)

parts.words: "My virtue's still far too small, I don't — it out and about yet" (Colette)
parts.note: Colette's quip treats her virtue like a pet or child not yet ready to be paraded around

explanation.surface: Colette joking that her virtue is too small to show in public.
explanation.definitionFit: To trot something out is to bring it forward for display.

clue.text: Carson McCullers's participant may have had something in common with the Ancient Mariner's audience

definitions.text: Carson McCullers's participant may have had something in common with the Ancient Mariner's audience

parts.words: Carson McCullers's participant may have had something in common with the Ancient Mariner's audience
parts.note: McCullers wrote a novel about a girl who longs to join her brother's marriage ceremony; Coleridge's Mariner stops a guest at one

explanation.surface: A McCullers character resembles the listener in Coleridge's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: McCullers's novel is The Member of the Wedding; the Ancient Mariner buttonholes a Wedding-Guest, so both belong to a wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Frankie wants to be part of the wedding party, like Coleridge's Wedding-Guest.

clue.text: Befuddled toper produces figurative expression

indicators.note: a befuddled drinker is confused, so the letters of toper are jumbled

explanation.surface: A muddled drunk comes out with a metaphor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Befuddled' rearranges TOPER.
explanation.definitionFit: A trope is a figure of speech such as metaphor or metonymy.

clue.text: "You meaner beauties of the night, /That poorly — our eyes" (Wotton)

definitions.text: "You meaner beauties of the night, /That poorly — our eyes" (Wotton)

parts.words: "You meaner beauties of the night, /That poorly — our eyes" (Wotton)
parts.note: Henry Wotton's poem to Elizabeth of Bohemia says the stars please the eyes only poorly beside her

explanation.surface: Wotton addressing the stars, which barely please us.
explanation.definitionFit: The stars only poorly content the eyes compared with the queen.

clue.text: Poor Terry gets fifty-fifty following for renegade Jesuit and a much-abused letter-writer

definitions.text: renegade Jesuit and a much-abused letter-writer

indicators.note: poor Terry is in a bad way, so the letters of that name are rearranged

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty, given twice

explanation.surface: Unlucky Terry gets an even share of supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' is the anagram signal, and fifty-fifty means two fifties in Roman numerals; 'following' is a link. George Tyrrell was a Catholic modernist expelled by the Jesuits in 1906.
explanation.definitionFit: George Tyrrell was a modernist priest expelled from the Jesuits; the definition joins a second bearer of the surname, a much-maligned correspondent.
